opus-5.5.text:
I think every founder has to be some mix of all three, but the proportions change depending on the stage of the company.

If I'm honest, my natural starting point is probably the visionary side. I came from mathematics, and in math you get used to staring at a problem that might take years and asking, "What would the world look like if this were solved?" So when I think about AI for mathematical reasoning, I'm very drawn to the long arc: a system that can prove things, check things, and eventually discover things humans haven't. That picture is what gets me out of bed.

But I learned quickly that vision alone is almost worthless at an early-stage company. Nobody joins you, and nobody funds you, because of a beautiful idea in your head. They join because they see you can execute: you hire the right people, set the right milestones, and ship something real on a timeline. So a lot of my energy now goes into being an executor. I break the big dream into concrete benchmarks, concrete systems, things we can measure in three months. Mathematicians are actually decent at this, because a proof is really a sequence of small, verifiable steps toward a big claim.

The salesperson part was the least natural for me. I used to think of "selling" as slightly uncomfortable, maybe a bit inauthentic. Over time I reframed it. Selling is really translation: taking something technical and explaining why it matters to a researcher I'm trying to recruit, to an investor, or to a future user. If I truly believe in what we're building, then explaining it clearly and with conviction isn't manipulation. It's part of the job. Recruiting especially is sales. The best people have many options, and you have to make them feel the mission.

So my answer is: visionary by temperament, executor by necessity, and salesperson by choice, because I realized the vision doesn't survive contact with reality unless you can bring other people into it.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, actually, because when I started Axiom I didn't fit neatly into any of those boxes, and I was a little anxious about that.

The way I see it, a visionary has conviction about where the world is going before the evidence is in. An executor turns that into something real, day after day, with discipline. And a salesperson gets other people to believe, whether that's investors, recruits, or customers. Most founders are strong in one, decent in a second, and have to hire for the third.

For me, the honest answer is that I started as a visionary with a mathematician's temperament. I'd spent years in pure math, and what I had was a very specific conviction: that formal reasoning, the kind where every step is machine-checkable, was going to matter enormously for AI, and that math was the right place to prove it. I could see the shape of it before most people cared. That's the visionary part.

What I had to learn, painfully, was execution. Research trains you to be comfortable with ambiguity and long timelines. Companies punish that. I had to become someone who decides on Tuesday, ships by Friday, and doesn't wait for the elegant proof. I think of myself now as an executor by necessity rather than by nature. I built habits around it rather than relying on instinct.

The salesperson part surprised me. I used to think of selling as somehow separate from the substance. But recruiting the people we have, convincing researchers to leave very comfortable positions, convincing investors that a tiny team could go after Fields-Medal-level problems, that was selling. And I found that when you genuinely believe the thing, selling is just explaining clearly and not flinching. So I'd say I'm a reluctant salesperson who turned out to be okay at it because I'm not pretending.

If I had to put weights on it, I'd say vision is my anchor, execution is what I've deliberately trained the hardest, and sales is the one I do only because the mission requires it. And I've tried to build a team where people are stronger than me in the second and third, so I don't have to be everything.

astra-6.text:
I think of those as three roles you have to move between, rather than three fixed types of people. The visionary asks, “What should exist?” The executor asks, “What can we do today to make it real?” And the salesperson asks, “How do I help someone else understand why this matters?”

I’d describe my own style as starting with a vision, but wanting to test it through execution. A compelling idea is a starting point; you still have to build something, learn from the response, and be willing to change your approach. And sales is part of that learning process. If you can’t explain the idea clearly, sometimes that means you haven’t understood it clearly enough yourself.

So I don’t aspire to be only one of those. I want to hold on to the ambition while being flexible about how we get there.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’m a mix, but I’m probably closest to a visionary who really cares about execution. I like asking, “What could exist that doesn’t exist yet?” But then I want to work backward: What would we have to build? Who would we need on the team? What can we test now?

And sales is part of that, because having a vision isn’t enough. You have to help other people understand why it matters and why they should join you. I don’t see those as three separate types of founders so much as three responsibilities. You might naturally gravitate toward one, but you still have to develop the others—and recognize where someone else can do it better.
